sections.h2: Which McCracken County offices touch a tax bill?
sections.html:
Three do, and none of them does another's job. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a dollar figure on every parcel. The Sheriff's Office takes in the money. The County Clerk steps in only when a bill goes unpaid past the spring cutoff. The PVA's website says outright that it neither mails bills nor accepts payments, so a check carried to the assessment office will be turned around.

You will find the PVA at 621 Washington Street in Paducah. Doors open at eight and close at four-thirty on weekdays, and the phone number is (270) 444-4712. Public service companies and a few similar accounts are valued in Frankfort by the state Revenue Cabinet instead. For payments, the Sheriff's tax page says the counter is staffed on weekdays from 8:30 until 4:30 while collection is open, and county government's address is 300 Clarence Gaines Street.

sections.h2: What is the payment calendar for McCracken County taxes?
sections.html:
Payment opens November 1 and ends April 15. The county's delinquent-tax FAQ says notices reach owners in late September or early October. KRS 134.015 then prices each stage:

  • Full payment by November 1 earns a 2 percent reduction, and that date for 2026 is behind us.
  • From November 2 through the end of December, you owe the bill as printed.
  • Throughout January, add 5 percent.
  • Once January ends, the add-on doubles to 10 percent.
  • On April 15 the Sheriff turns over whatever is still open.

The Sheriff accepts payments in person, by mail, by phone and through a web button that the office says is live from November to April. Card and e-check users pay a processing fee to an outside vendor, quoted before the transaction is final. Homeowners with an escrow account should call the lender first, because the Sheriff mails a bill to the owner only, and the lender may already have requested its own copy.

sections.h2: How much will a McCracken County tax bill come to?
sections.html:
For 2025 Frankfort set its own share at 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value, trimmed from 10.9 cents a year earlier. Run that against the $188,100 Census median and you get about $199.39 for the state alone. The city, schools, library, fire districts and county each add a levy, and the PVA lists those same bodies as users of its assessments.

One line on the bill is new. Starting with the 2024 bills, a county 911 fee appears, and the Sheriff's page says most parcels pay $46.26 for it. The early-payment reduction skips that line, which matters when you estimate a credit at closing.

sections.h2: What steps does a McCracken County owner follow to contest a value?
sections.html:
A sit-down at the PVA office comes first, since no appeal is accepted without one. After that the clock runs on a fixed calendar.

  • For 13 days from the first Monday in May, the roll is open to anyone who wants to look.
  • Your conference with the PVA or a deputy should end with a written record of what each side said.
  • The appeal then goes to the County Clerk no later than the next workday after viewing ends.
  • Gather proof for the hearing: insurance papers, building costs, land and structure descriptions, and sale listings. A claim with nothing attached is rejected.
  • A board of local owners hears the case roughly a month after viewing ends.

Anyone paid to speak for you needs to fall into a category the Revenue Department recognizes, such as attorney, CPA or certified appraiser, and must hold your signed authorization. When a board sets the value above what you claimed after bills have gone out, you receive a supplemental bill. The Sheriff adds a caution of its own: leaving new additions off the record can bring a 20 percent penalty on the bill.

sections.h2: Can older McCracken County owners lower the taxable value?
sections.html:
Yes. Owners 65 and over, along with those found totally disabled, can claim a $49,100 deduction for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. The state subtracts it before any rate is applied.

Take the $188,100 median: taxable value falls to $139,000, and the state's slice drops to about $147.34. The application goes to the McCracken County PVA rather than the Sheriff. A birth certificate, driver's license or passport shows age. Claimants who rely on disability must have a federal or retirement-system finding, and most renew yearly. The exceptions are veterans with a service-connected disability and people whom Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement Systems have ruled permanently and totally disabled. The PVA's site says a formal application must be filed before any exemption is granted.

sections.h2: What becomes of an unpaid McCracken County bill when the house is sold?
sections.html:
It stays on the parcel. Past April 15 the bill turns into a certificate of delinquency held by the County Clerk, a lien goes on record, and interest accrues at 1 percent each month. Under KRS 134.420 that lien can last 11 years even after a transfer, so a title search will surface it.

Collection is run by the County Attorney under an agreement with the state revenue department. The attorney's letters warn that continued non-payment can lead to foreclosure, while an owner who keeps up an installment agreement has the bill marked unavailable for sale to investors. The Clerk's yearly sale of such bills is normally held in October. An investor who buys one must notify the owner within 50 days, may add its own charges, and can ask a court to foreclose after a year. Before you list, ask the Sheriff for a payoff and clear it ahead of April 15 if you can.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about McCracken County itself?
sections.html:
The county spreads over 268 square miles at Kentucky's far western tip, part of the Jackson Purchase, with the Ohio River along its north and the Tennessee River along its northeast. It dates from 1825 and anchors the Paducah, KY-IL metropolitan area. Paducah, the seat, is the lone incorporated city. Farley, Hendron, Massac and Reidland are census-designated places, and names such as Lone Oak, Heath and West Paducah show up as unincorporated communities.

Steamboats, barges and the Illinois Central made this a river-and-rail economy, and the railroad built what Wikipedia calls the largest operating and maintenance base in the world here in the 1920s. McCracken County Public Schools covers most of the county, Paducah Public Schools serves most of the city, and West Kentucky Community and Technical College sits in Paducah. Clocks run on Central time, and workers report a mean trip to work of 17.6 minutes.

About 69 percent of homes are lived in by owners, and with 170 permits issued in 2025, most sales involve a house that already stands. If yours carries back taxes, a lien or repairs you would rather not fund, a buyer who pays cash and takes the house as-is can settle the tax payoff and the sale in one closing.

faqs.q: Can I pay my McCracken County property tax at the PVA office?
faqs.a: No. The PVA values property and processes exemptions. Payments go to the Sheriff's Office.

faqs.q: What happens on April 15 to McCracken County taxes?
faqs.a: Collection by the Sheriff ends at closing time that day. Whatever is unpaid goes to the County Clerk, and interest and fees begin to build.

faqs.q: Does the 2 percent early-pay reduction cover the 911 fee?
faqs.a: It does not. The Sheriff's page says the 911 fee, added with the 2024 bills, sits outside the reduction, and most parcels pay $46.26.

faqs.q: What is the McCracken County homestead deduction for 2026?
faqs.a: It is $49,100, the same figure used for 2025. Owners 65 or over, or totally disabled, apply through the PVA.

faqs.q: Can a McCracken County house with delinquent tax still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is normally paid from the proceeds at closing, or a buyer takes the house with the lien attached. Get a payoff from the Sheriff or Clerk first.
